title: Entanglement in Presence of Topological Interfaces and Dualities
authors: Christian Northe, Riccardo Poletti, Paolo Rossi
abstract: Entanglement through interfaces has attracted considerable attention in 2d conformal field theory (CFT). However, it is known that field-theoretic predictions based on the existing framework are in general incompatible with numerical results [1-4]. A new framework for entanglement through topological defects was recently proposed in [5]. It provides a general description of entanglement through topological defects and successfully reproduces the numerical results for the Ising model in all tested cases and regimes. The key insight is that the relevant quantum correlations are encoded in twisted states, allowing for the construction of the full reduced density matrix (RDM). In this work we pursue two objectives. First, we provide new examples by studying defects in the free boson CFT. Second, we extend the framework to topological interfaces connecting two, possibly distinct, CFTs. Of particular interest are interfaces relating dual theories. We show that the reduced density matrix for a duality interface is the projection of the vacuum reduced density matrix onto a single symmetry sector, closely paralleling the framework of symmetry resolution. Unlike symmetry resolution, however, the projection is imposed by the physical interface itself, demonstrating that duality interfaces reflect quantum correlations back into the entangling interval. We establish this mechanism for diagonal and non-diagonal rational CFTs as well as the free boson CFT. Relative entropy allows us to quantify the distinguishability of the duality interface RDM from the vacuum RDM.
summary: This paper develops a generalized framework for calculating entanglement across topological interfaces connecting different Conformal Field Theories. The key finding is that duality interfaces project the system's quantum correlations onto specific symmetry sectors, mirroring symmetry resolution but arising naturally from the physical boundary itself. This provides a rigorous tool to quantify how dual theories constrain quantum information at their junction.
main_problem: The work extends the theory of entanglement through topological defects/interfaces, specifically focusing on interfaces connecting two distinct Conformal Field Theories (CFTs), particularly when these theories are dual to each other.
main_result: For duality interfaces, the reduced density matrix acts as a projector onto a fixed-charge subsector of the vacuum's entanglement spectrum, naturally reflecting quantum correlations back into the entangling interval.
method: The authors utilize a framework involving 'twisted states' to construct the full reduced density matrix (RDM) and employ relative entropy to quantify the distinguishability between the interface RDM and the vacuum RDM.
model_or_system: The study is set in 1+1 dimensional CFTs, with specific examples including the free boson CFT and systems exhibiting duality relations (e.g., Kramers-Wannier or T-duality).
key_observables: Reduced Density Matrix (RDM), Entanglement Entropy ($S$), Relative Entropy, and the entanglement spectrum.
important_parameters: The nature of the CFTs (diagonal/non-diagonal rational, free boson) and the specific type of interface (duality vs. general).
main_assumptions: Previous foundational theories for interface entropies are noted to be incompatible with numerical results; the framework extends prior work on defects to distinct CFT interfaces.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the mapping between two phases P and Q connected by an interface I (and $\bar{I}$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework for entanglement through topological defects, then applies it to study interfaces connecting distinct CFTs, culminating in a detailed analysis of how duality interfaces project quantum correlations.
why_interesting: The mechanism described—where physical boundaries naturally impose symmetry constraints on entanglement—provides a powerful theoretical tool applicable to understanding boundary effects and correlation structure in complex many-body systems beyond simple thermalization assumptions.
